subtype: Approach: uses safe cheap trials when testing is inexpensive and mistakes are recoverable [Thinking]
passage: With a tight food budget and one gas ring in the shared flat, Harsha, who had just started cooking for her flatmates, could not afford a ruined big batch of dal. So she filled four small pots with a cup of dal each and changed one thing in each: an extra pinch of turmeric, a little more cumin, lemon at the end, a tempering of garlic. Ankita, a flatmate, tasted each from a steel spoon and said, 'Number three.' Harsha wrote on the back of an envelope: cumin plus garlic. Pots one and four went into lunch boxes so nothing was wasted. Next day Harsha made a full pot with that mix and it tasted right.

qa.q: How many small pots did Harsha fill?
What was Harsha afraid of when choosing small pots?
qa.a: Harsha was afraid of ruining a big batch on a tight budget, so she wanted cheap trials that could be undone.

qa.q: What other approach could Harsha use to remember the recipe?
qa.a: Harsha could measure the spices in spoonfuls and write the amounts down, since a written recipe makes the good pot easy to repeat.

qa.q: How might Ankita have seen the tasting?
qa.a: Ankita probably enjoyed being part of it, and gave a clear choice by saying 'Number three.'

grounding: Shows a new cook trying spice changes in several small pots of dal instead of one big batch, so mistakes are cheap and reversible.
